title: When the Saints Go Marching In
origin: American gospel hymn turned New Orleans brass band standard

pd.detail: In print by 1896 as 'When the Saints Are Marching In', words Katharine E. Purvis, music James M. Black; the marching tune encoded here also circulated as anonymous gospel and brass band material in the same period, so on either attribution the composition was published well before 1930.
pd.sourceEdition: Purvis / Black, 'When the Saints Are Marching In', 1896 gospel song sheet; head encoded in the standard New Orleans brass band 16-bar reading
pd.notes: Melody and harmony only; no lyrics are carried. Whether the modern marching tune is Black's 1896 melody or an older anonymous one is disputed, and the file takes no position: both routes are clear of copyright. Encoded as the traditional brass band head, never any single recorded arrangement (Louis Armstrong's 1938 reading and later versions carry their own arrangement copyrights).

notes: Brass band folios write this in cut time; mapped bar for bar to 4/4 with the tempo given in 4/4 quarter notes. The head is a 16-bar chorus in four 4-bar lines (A A B A). Each line's three-note rising pickup (1 3 4) lives at the END of the preceding section, per SPEC, so every melodic entry gets it. The A line is 5 held / 3 / 1 / 3 / 2 held, the long 2 carrying most of bars 2-3; the Head Out resolves that 2 down to a held 1. The B line ('Oh Lord I want to be in that number') is shipped as a chord-only break for the band to answer over rather than guessing at its note-level reading. Harmony is the standard three-chord reading with V7 under each line's held note; folios that hold I through the whole first line put a bar-long 9th over F, which is why V7 is used here. Confidence is medium because one of the four lines is deliberately absent and the phrase rhythm follows the common brass band reading rather than a single printed score.
